claim: Dementia is associated with severe spatial memory deficits which arise from dysfunction in hippocampal and parahippocampal circuits.
source: Dementia is associated with severe spatial memory deficits which arise from dysfunction in hippocampal and parahippocampal circuits.
evidence: This is a general statement about dementia that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Grid cell firing patterns are largely absent in rTg4510 mice.
source: We find that grid cell firing patterns are largely absent in rTg4510 mice, while head-direction tuning remains largely intact.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 3 showing grid scores and proportions of grid cells.

claim: Head-direction tuning remains largely intact in rTg4510 mice.
source: We find that grid cell firing patterns are largely absent in rTg4510 mice, while head-direction tuning remains largely intact.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5 showing head-direction scores.

claim: Neural representation of running speed information was significantly disturbed in rTg4510 mice, with smaller proportions of MEC cells having firing rates correlated with locomotion.
source: Conversely, neural representation of running speed information was significantly disturbed, with smaller proportions of MEC cells having firing rates correlated with locomotion in rTg4510 mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4 showing speed scores and proportions of speed-modulated cells.

claim: The power of local field potential oscillations in the theta and gamma frequency bands was invariant in rTg4510 mice during locomotion.
source: Additionally, the power of local field potential oscillations in the theta and gamma frequency bands, which in wild-type mice are tightly linked to running speed, was invariant in rTg4510 mice during locomotion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1 showing oscillation power-running speed relationships.

claim: In wild-type mice, theta and gamma oscillation power is tightly linked to running speed.
source: Additionally, the power of local field potential oscillations in the theta and gamma frequency bands, which in wild-type mice are tightly linked to running speed, was invariant in rTg4510 mice during locomotion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1 and is consistent with established knowledge in the field.

claim: Deficits in locomotor speed encoding likely severely impact path integration systems in dementia.
source: These deficits in locomotor speed encoding likely severely impact path integration systems in dementia.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Place cells in the hippocampus fire action potentials in specific spatial locations.
source: For example, place cells in the hippocampus fire action potentials in specific spatial locations (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex fire in a highly organised, hexagonally distributed spatial pattern across an environment.
source: whereas grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) fire in a highly organised, hexagonally distributed spatial pattern across an environment (Fyhn et al., 2004; Hafting et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The MEC contains head-direction cells.
source: These directly spatially sensitive neurons are collocated within the MEC with other functionally defined cell types, including head-direction (HD; Giocomo et al., 2014; Sargolini et al., 2006; Ranck, 1984; Valerio and Taube, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The MEC contains speed cells.
source: These directly spatially sensitive neurons are collocated within the MEC with other functionally defined cell types, including head-direction (HD; Giocomo et al., 2014; Sargolini et al., 2006; Ranck, 1984; Valerio and Taube, 2012), speed (Kropff et al., 2015; Hinman et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The MEC contains border cells.
source: These directly spatially sensitive neurons are collocated within the MEC with other functionally defined cell types, including head-direction (HD; Giocomo et al., 2014; Sargolini et al., 2006; Ranck, 1984; Valerio and Taube, 2012), speed (Kropff et al., 2015; Hinman et al., 2016), and border cells (Lever et al., 2009; Solstad et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Grid cells, head-direction cells, speed cells, and border cells together provide the crucial computational information required for effective path integration.
source: Together these are thought to provide the crucial computational information required for effective path integration, the process of using idiothetic cues to continuously calculate positional information (Barry and Bush, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents a theoretical framework in the field.

claim: Patients with Alzheimer's disease exhibit profound disruption in spatial navigation and memory, even at very early stages of the disease.
source: Patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and other dementia-spectrum disorders exhibit profound disruption in spatial navigation and memory, even at very early stages of the disease (Allison et al., 2016; Lithfous et al., 2013; Hort et al., 2007; Laczó et al., 2011; Mokrisova et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Misfolded tau deposition typically occurs first in the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus.
source: At a pathological level, misfolded tau deposition typically occurs first in the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus (Pooler et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Dementia pathologies can disrupt the intrinsic properties of pyramidal cells in area CA1 of the hippocampus.
source: In this regard, there is substantial evidence from transgenic mouse models that dementia pathologies, such as β-amyloid deposition (Aβ) and hyperphosphorylation and misfolding of tau, can disrupt the intrinsic properties (Booth et al., 2016a; Tamagnini et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2011; Kerrigan et al., 2014) and synaptic microcircuits (Hoover et al., 2010; Brown et al., 2005; Fitzjohn et al., 2001) of pyramidal cells in area CA1 of the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Dementia pathologies can disrupt synaptic microcircuits of pyramidal cells in area CA1 of the hippocampus.
source: In this regard, there is substantial evidence from transgenic mouse models that dementia pathologies, such as β-amyloid deposition (Aβ) and hyperphosphorylation and misfolding of tau, can disrupt the intrinsic properties (Booth et al., 2016a; Tamagnini et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2011; Kerrigan et al., 2014) and synaptic microcircuits (Hoover et al., 2010; Brown et al., 2005; Fitzjohn et al., 2001) of pyramidal cells in area CA1 of the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Place cells in the CA1 region of APP and tau overexpressing mice have reduced spatial-sensitivity.
source: Furthermore, there is growing evidence that place cells in the CA1 region of APP and tau overexpressing mice have reduced spatial-sensitivity (Booth et al., 2016a; Cheng and Ji, 2013; Cacucci et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The circuits required for generation of theta and gamma frequency oscillations in the dorsal entorhinal cortex are especially prone to dysfunction in rTg4510 mice.
source: Recent evidence suggests that the circuits required for generation of theta and gamma frequency oscillations in the dorsal entorhinal cortex are especially prone to dysfunction in a mouse model of tauopathy (rTg4510 mice) (Booth et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Grid cell spatial periodicity is reduced in mice where tau overexpression is restricted to the entorhinal cortex.
source: Furthermore, Fu et al., 2017 demonstrated that grid cell spatial periodicity is reduced in mice where tau overexpression is restricted to the entorhinal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Human imaging studies suggest deficits in grid-cell-like activity in the entorhinal cortices of people at genetic risk of developing AD.
source: These data correlate with human imaging studies which suggest deficits in grid-cell-like activity in the entorhinal cortices of people at genetic risk of developing AD (Kunz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In WT mice, theta oscillation power is positively correlated with running speed (R2 = 0.71, p<0.001, n = 7 mice).
source: Pooled data illustrate a clear relationship between running speed and theta oscillation power (linear regression: R2 = 0.71, p<0.001, n = 7 mice)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In WT mice, theta oscillation frequency is positively correlated with running speed (R2 = 0.69, p<0.001, n = 7 mice).
source: Pooled data illustrate a clear relationship between running speed and theta oscillation power (linear regression: R2 = 0.71, p<0.001, n = 7 mice) and frequency (linear regression: R2 = 0.69, p<0.001, n = 7 mice) (Figure 1Ci).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In rTg4510 mice, theta oscillation amplitude was poorly correlated with locomotor activity (R2 = 0.15, p=0.02, n = 8 mice).
source: In contrast, in rTg4510 mice, theta oscillation amplitude was poorly correlated with locomotor activity and remained at consistent levels throughout recording sessions (linear regression: R2 = 0.15, p=0.02, n = 8 mice, Figure 1Ci).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The Z-transformed correlation coefficient for theta power-running speed relationships was significantly lower in rTg4510 mice when compared to WT controls.
source: Importantly the overall Z-transformed correlation coefficient and slope relationships for theta power-running speed relationships were significantly lower in rTg4510 mice when compared to WT controls (two-way repeated measures ANOVA, see Table 1 and Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Table 1 and Figure 1D.

claim: The slope of theta power-running speed relationships was significantly lower in rTg4510 mice when compared to WT controls.
source: Importantly the overall Z-transformed correlation coefficient and slope relationships for theta power-running speed relationships were significantly lower in rTg4510 mice when compared to WT controls (two-way repeated measures ANOVA, see Table 1 and Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Table 1 and Figure 1D.

claim: Peak theta frequency was correlated with running speed in rTg4510 mice (R2 = 0.74, p<0.01, n = 8 mice).
source: Although less pronounced than in WT animals, peak theta frequency was correlated with running speed in rTg4510 mice (linear regression: R2 = 0.74, p<0.01, n = 8 mice, Figure 1Cii)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The correlation between theta frequency and running speed was not significantly different between WT and rTg4510 mice (WT: 0.84 ± 0.24, rTg4510: 0.40 ± 0.14, unpaired T-test, p=0.13, n = 7/8 mice).
source: which across the population was not significantly different from WT (Correlation (Z'); WT: 0.84 ± 0.24, rTg4510: 0.40 ± 0.14, unpaired T-test, p=0.13, n = 7/8 mice)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In WT mice, fast gamma oscillation power was positively correlated with running speed (R2 = 0.90, p<0.001, n = 7 mice).
source: In WT mice, both fast and slow gamma oscillation power was positively correlated with running speed (linear regression; fast gamma: R2 = 0.90, p<0.001, n = 7 mice; slow gamma: R2 = 0.17 p=0.013, n = 8 mice)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In WT mice, slow gamma oscillation power was positively correlated with running speed (R2 = 0.17 p=0.013, n = 8 mice).
source: In WT mice, both fast and slow gamma oscillation power was positively correlated with running speed (linear regression; fast gamma: R2 = 0.90, p<0.001, n = 7 mice; slow gamma: R2 = 0.17 p=0.013, n = 8 mice)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: rTg4510 mice did not show significant correlations for fast gamma frequency band oscillations (R2 = 0.03, p=0.67, n = 8 mice).
source: rTg4510 mice did not show significant correlations for fast gamma frequency band oscillations (linear regression; fast gamma: R2 = 0.03, p=0.67, n = 8 mice, Figure 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: rTg4510 mice showed significant correlations for slow gamma frequencies (R2 = 0.43, p<0.01, n = 8 mice).
source: but did for slow gamma frequencies (R2 = 0.43, p<0.01, n = 8 mice, Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: rTg4510 mice display a hyperactive phenotype under various conditions, which becomes more pronounced with developing tau pathology.
source: rTg4510 mice have been shown to display a hyperactive phenotype under various conditions, which becomes more pronounced with developing tau pathology (Selenica et al., 2014; Cook et al., 2014; Jul et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: rTg4510 mice spent more time at faster running speeds and had greater average speeds across recording sessions than WT control mice (p=0.04, Unpaired T-test, n = 8/10).
source: rTg4510 mice were shown to spend more time at faster running speed, with average speeds across recording sessions greater than WT control mice (p=0.04, Unpaired T-test, n = 8/10, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A total of 279 single-units were isolated in layer II/III of the dorsal MEC from 10 mice (WT:150 units from five mice, rTg4510: 129 units from five mice).
source: To establish whether this was the case, we used high-density silicone probes to isolate a total of 279 single-units in layer II/III of the dorsal MEC from 10 mice (WT:150 units from five mice, rTg4510: 129 units from five mice).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data collected.

claim: Estimated recording location was not different between genotypes (Median distance from dorsal entorhinal border (IQR): WT: 350(350) μm, rTg4510: 385(275) μm, U = 9660, p=0.77, Mann-Whitney U test).
source: Importantly, estimated recording location was not different between genotypes (Median distance from dorsal entorhinal border (interquartile range (IQR)): WT: 350(350) μm, rTg4510: 385(275) μm, U = 9660, p=0.77, Mann-Whitney U test Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: MEC single units recorded from rTg4510 mice exhibited a decrease in mean firing rate (Median (IQR): WT: 2.97 (16.7) Hz, rTg4510: 1.03 (3.0) Hz, U = 4472, p=0.01, Mann-Whitney U, n = 150; 129 units).
source: Considered across the entire cellular population, MEC single units recorded from rTg4510 mice exhibited a decrease in mean firing rate (Median (IQR): WT: 2.97 (16.7) Hz, rTg4510: 1.03 (3.0) Hz, U = 4472, p=0.01, Mann-Whitney U, n = 150; 129 units, Figure 2A/B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: rTg4510 cells showed a pronounced decrease in theta modulation of firing patterns (Median (IQR) theta modulation index: WT: 9.17 (13.9), rTg4510: 2.29 (2.81), U = 2296, p<0.001, Mann-Whitney U, n = 150;129 units).
source: As in the CA1 region of the hippocampus (Booth et al., 2016a), rTg4510 cells also showed a pronounced decrease in theta modulation of firing patterns (Median (IQR) theta modulation index: WT: 9.17 (13.9), rTg4510: 2.29 (2.81), U = 2296, p<0.001, Mann-Whitney U, n = 150;129 units, Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 65% of WT MEC cells showed significant theta modulation, while only 13% passed threshold in rTg4510 mice (χ² (1)=64.1, p<0.0001, Chi-Square test).
source: Although the majority of WT MEC cells (65%) showed significant theta modulation, only a small proportion (13%) passed threshold in rTg4510 mice (χ² (1)=64.1, p<0.0001, Chi-Square test, Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 31% of units in WT mice were classed as putative interneurons, whereas in rTg4510 mice 15% were classed as putative interneurons (χ² (1)=16.0, p<0.001, Chi-Square test).
source: Using this approach, we found that 47/150 units (31%) were classed as putative interneurons in WT mice, where as in rTg4510 mice a significantly smaller proportion of units were classed as putative interneurons (19/129 units, 15%; χ² (1)=16.0, p<0.001, Chi-Square test; Figure 2E/F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2E/F.

claim: ~1/4 of cells in the WT MEC had grid-like spatial firing patterns in a 0.8 m x 0.8 m square arena.
source: Consistent with the literature we found that ~1/4 of cells in the WT MEC had grid-like spatial firing patterns in a 0.8 m x 0.8 m square arena (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison to literature.

claim: 36/150 cells (24%) in WT mice had grid scores higher than the 95th percentile of the distribution produced from shuffled spike timestamps (threshold = 0.21).
source: We calculated a grid score for each cell, based on the rotational symmetry of the 2D-autocorrelations and found that 36/150 cells (24%) had grid scores higher than the 95th percentile of the distribution produced from shuffled spike timestamps (threshold = 0.21; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In rTg4510 mice there was an almost complete breakdown of grid cell periodicity (3/129 units, 2.3%, threshold: 0.26) (χ² (1)=27.1, p<0.0001, Chi-Square test).
source: In contrast, in rTg4510 mice there was an almost complete breakdown of grid cell periodicity (3/129 units, 2.3%, threshold: 0.26), with animals displaying irregular, non-uniform, firing fields across recording environments (χ² (1)=27.1, p<0.0001, Chi-Square test, Figure 3A/C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The distribution of grid scores of all cells recorded from WT and rTg4510 mice was significantly different (Median (IQR) grid score: WT, 0.03 (0.3); rTg4510, 0 (0.12), n = 150/129 units; p<0.001; Mann-Whitney U).
source: Furthermore, the distribution of grid scores of all cells recorded from WT and rTg4510 mice was significantly different (Median (IQR) grid score: WT, 0.03 (0.3); rTg4510, 0 (0.12), n = 150/129 units; p<0.001; Mann-Whitney U, Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: MEC neurons did not differ significantly between genotypes in spatial information content (WT, 0.36 (0.75) bits/spike, n = 150; rTg4510, 0.49 (0.53) bits/spike, n = 129 units; p=0.38; Mann-Whitney U).
source: Conversely, when measuring the spatial information content (SI) of recorded cells (Skaggs et al., 1993), we found that MEC neurons did not differ significantly between genotypes, either as a distribution (WT, 0.36 (0.75) bits/spike, n = 150; rTg4510, 0.49 (0.53) bits/spike, n = 129 units; p=0.38; Mann-Whitney U, Figure 3E)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: rTg4510 MEC units displayed a significantly lower average speed score compared to WT mice (Median (IQR): WT: z = 0.11 (0.31), rTg4510: z = 0.009 (0.01), U = 3603, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney U, n = 150;129 units).
source: As an overall population, rTg4510 MEC units also displayed a significantly lower average speed score compared to WT mice (Median (IQR): WT: z = 0.11 (0.31), rTg4510: z = 0.009 (0.01), U = 3603, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney U, n = 150;129 units, Figure 4E)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In WT animals, speed-modulated cells showed an approximately equal distribution between linear and saturating running speed relationships (linear: 41/85 units, saturating: 44/85 units).
source: In WT animals, speed-modulated cells showed an approximately equal distribution between linear and saturating running speed relationships (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 linear: 41/85 units, saturating: 44/85 units)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In rTg4510 mice, the proportion of cells with negative speed relationships was substantially and significantly higher than in WT mice (WT: 11/85 units, rTg4510: 7/17 units, χ² (1)=7.8, p=0.005, Chi-Square test).
source: In contrast, in rTg4510 mice the proportion of cells with negative speed relationships was substantially and significantly higher (WT: 11/85 units, rTg4510: 7/17 units, χ² (1)=7.8, p=0.005, Chi-Square test, Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In WT mice, CA1 theta band activity in the local field potential was correlated with running speed (linear regression; theta power; WT: R2 = 0.83, p<0.001, n = 6 mice).
source: In this region, CA1 theta band activity in the local field potential was also correlated with running speed in WT mice (linear regression; theta power; WT: R2 = 0.83, p<0.001, n = 6 mice)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In rTg4510 mice, CA1 theta band activity in the local field potential was not correlated with running speed (linear regression: R2 = −0.04, p=0.6, n = 4 mice).
source: but not in rTg4510 mice (linear regression: R2 = −0.04, p=0.6, n = 4 mice, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A significant proportion of CA1 neurons had firing rates modulated by running speed in both WT and rTg4510 mice (WT: 25/46 units, rTg4510: 27/52 units).
source: A significant proportion of CA1 neurons had firing rates modulated by running speed in both WT and rTg4510 mice (WT: 25/46 units, rTg4510: 27/52 units).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A much greater proportion of CA1 cells were negatively modulated by locomotor activity in rTg4510 mice than in WT controls (WT: 5/25 units, rTg4510:13/27 units; χ² (1)=4.5, p=0.03, Chi-Square test).
source: Importantly however, as seen in MEC recordings, a much greater proportion of CA1 cells were negatively modulated by locomotor activity in rTg4510 mice than in WT controls (WT: 5/25 units, rTg4510:13/27 units; χ² (1)=4.5, p=0.03, Chi-Square test, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A similar proportion of MEC cells in WT and rTg4510 mice surpassed the 95th-centile threshold for head-direction scores (WT: 19/150, rTg4510: 14/129, χ² (1)=0.79, p=0.37, Chi-Square test).
source: Importantly, a similar proportion of MEC cells in WT and rTg4510 mice surpassed the 95th-centile threshold (WT: 19/150, rTg4510: 14/129, χ² (1)=0.79, p=0.37, Chi-Square test, Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The HD score was slightly but significantly higher in rTg4510 cells compared to WT (Median (IQR) vector length: WT: 0.074 (0.091), rTg4510: 0.11 (0.12), U = 6509, p=0.0014, Mann-Whitney U, n = 150;129 units).
source: Furthermore, as a population, the HD score was actually slightly, but significantly, higher in rTg4510 cells compared to WT (Median (IQR) vector length: WT: 0.074 (0.091), rTg4510: 0.11 (0.12), U = 6509, p=0.0014, Mann-Whitney U, n = 150;129 units, Figure 5B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Healthy grid cells are largely resistant to decreases in firing rate until firing rates are decreased to an average of ~0.1 Hz.
source: As reported previously (Bonnevie et al., 2013), healthy grid cells are largely resistent to such decreases in firing, until firing rates are decreased to an average of ~0.1 Hz (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no difference in the average grid score between session halves for either WT (Z = −0.2, p=0.82; Wilcoxon signed ranks test) or rTg4510 mice (Z = 1.6, p=0.11; Wilcoxon signed ranks test).
source: We found no difference in the average grid score between session halves for either WT (Z = −0.2, p=0.82; Wilcoxon signed ranks test) or rTg4510 mice (Z = 1.6, p=0.11; Wilcoxon signed ranks test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Speed scores were stable across sessions in both WT (Z = −0.77, p=0.44; Wilcoxon signed ranks test) and rTg4510 mice (Z = 1.6, p=0.10; Wilcoxon signed ranks test).
source: The same was true for speed scores, which were also stable across sessions in both WT (Z = −0.77, p=0.44; Wilcoxon signed ranks test) and rTg4510 mice (Z = 1.6, p=0.10; Wilcoxon signed ranks test)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: HD scores from rTg4510 mice were slightly but significantly increased in the second half of the recording session, compared to the first (Z = −4.35,p=0.0001; Wilcoxon signed ranks test).
source: However, whilst HD firing appears to be intact in rTg4510 mice, HD scores from transgenic mice were slightly, but significantly increased in the second half of the recording session, compared to the first (Z = −4.35,p=0.0001; Wilcoxon signed ranks test)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: WT HD cells remained constant through each recording session (Z = −1.6, p=0.10; Wilcoxon signed ranks test).
source: while WT cells remained constant through each recording session (Z = −1.6, p=0.10; Wilcoxon signed ranks test)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: rTg4510 HD cells were significantly more variable within sessions when compared to WT controls (Median (IQR) HD score difference (2nd−1st half), WT: 0.01 (0.11), rTg4510: 0.06 (0.14), p=0.001, Mann-Whitney U, n = 150; 129 units).
source: Comparing between genotypes, rTg4510 cells were also significantly more variable within sessions when compared to WT controls (Median (IQR) HD score difference (2nd−1st half), WT: 0.01 (0.11), rTg4510: 0.06 (0.14), p=0.001, Mann-Whitney U, n = 150; 129 units, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: ~60% of WT cells passed the threshold for only a single functional class of neuron (i.e. grid-, speed-, or HD-cells).
source: Using the tuning-curve approaches defined above, we found that ~60% of WT cells passed the threshold for only a single functional class of neuron (i.e. grid-, speed-, or HD-cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: ~25% of WT cells passed the threshold for more than one functional class and were therefore conjunctive cells.
source: A further ~25% of WT cells passed the threshold for more than one functional class and were therefore conjunctive cells, whilst the remaining ~20% of cells were unclassified (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Only 3% of spatially sensitive cells in WT mice were pure grid cells.
source: For example, in this study, only 3% of spatially sensitive cells were pure grid cells, whilst the remaining grid cells also passed the threshold for speed- and HD-modulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Very few rTg4510 cells (~2%) expressed any conjunctive representation.
source: In contrast, due to the substantial reduction in numbers of speed and grid cells, very few rTg4510 cells (~2%) expressed any conjunctive representation (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Continuous integration of running speed information in the MEC has been proposed to be critically important for spatial navigation and path integration.
source: Continuous integration of running speed information in the MEC has been proposed to be critically important for spatial navigation and path integration (Sargolini et al., 2006; Kropff et al., 2015; McNaughton et al., 2006; Burgess et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Reduced grid cell periodicity may be the result of the impaired integration of running speed information in the MEC.
source: Our data suggest the hypothesis that reduced grid cell periodicity may be the result of the impaired integration of running speed information in the MEC.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings.

claim: Inhibition of the medial septum produces a complete breakdown of grid cell periodicity.
source: For example, inhibition of the medial septum, which controls theta rhythmicity, but also speed-modulated inputs, produces a complete breakdown of grid cell periodicity (Brandon et al., 2011; Koenig et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Inactivation of the anterior thalamic nuclei disrupts HD tuning in the MEC and impairs the grid cell signal.
source: Likewise, inactivation of the anterior thalamic nuclei (ATN) disrupts HD tuning in the MEC, also impairing the grid cell signal (Winter et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Inactivation of reciprocal hippocampal inputs into the MEC is sufficient to produce a breakdown in grid cell periodicity.
source: Inactivation of reciprocal hippocampal inputs into the MEC is also sufficient to produce a breakdown in grid cell periodicity (Bonnevie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Mice lacking GluA1-containing AMPA receptors display reduced grid cell periodicity, correlating with impairments on a path integration-based task.
source: For example, mice lacking GluA1-containing AMPA receptors have been shown to display reduced grid cell periodicity, correlating with impairments on a path integration-based task (Allen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Path integration has been suggested to be impaired in populations of dementia and MCI patients.
source: Path integration has also been suggested to be impaired in populations of dementia and MCI patients (Allison et al., 2016; Hort et al., 2007; Mokrisova et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Blocking medial septum activity impairs grid cell firing, but not HD tuning.
source: Blocking medial septum activity impairs grid cell firing, but not HD tuning (Brandon et al., 2011; Koenig et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The breakdown of grid periodicity after hippocampal inactivation reveals HD tuning in grid cells that would previously not have been modulated by HD.
source: Interestingly, the breakdown of grid periodicity after hippocampal inactivation has also been shown to reveal HD tuning in grid cells that would previously not have been modulated by HD (Bonnevie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The arrival of HD information into the MEC is likely the result of an anatomically distinct pathway that appears to be relatively preserved in the face of the tau pathology burden in rTg4510 mice at this stage.
source: In any case, the arrival of HD information into the MEC is likely the result of an anatomically distinct pathway (Taube, 2007) that appears to be relatively preserved in the face of the tau pathology burden in rTg4510 mice at this stage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and a citation to prior work.

claim: The HD pathway is most likely preserved due to a greater dependence on subcortical structures, such as the ATN, that integrate vestibular information.
source: This is most likely due to a greater dependence on subcortical structures, such as the ATN, that integrate vestibular information (Stackman and Taube, 1998; Blair et al., 2007; Sharp et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and citations to prior work.

claim: Theta oscillations exhibit increases in both amplitude and frequency depending on running speed.
source: Theta oscillations exhibit increases in both amplitude and frequency depending on running speed (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and is consistent with established knowledge.

claim: In rTg4510 mice, theta oscillation power appears to be independent of running speed.
source: In rTg4510 mice, theta oscillation power appears to be independent of running speed meaning that these animals are unable to integrate this information effectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The MEC provides the input responsible for fast gamma frequencies in CA1 region of the hippocampus.
source: This is consistent with the proposed information flow across the hippocampal formation, in which the MEC provides the input responsible for fast gamma frequencies in CA1 region of the hippocampus (Colgin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: MEC LFP predominantly contains faster gamma frequencies only.
source: While the CA1 area has been shown to display two distinct peaks in the gamma band power spectra, MEC LFP predominantly contains faster gamma frequencies only (Colgin et al., 2009; Chrobak and Buzsáki, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: rTg4510 mice exhibit a hyperactive phenotype.
source: It is also worth noting that rTg4510 mice, like several other models of dementia, exhibit a hyperactive phenotype (Blackmore et al., 2017; Jul et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2014; Przybyla et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rTg(tet-o-TauP301L)4510 mouse model expresses a repressible form of human tau containing the P301L mutation that has been linked with familial frontotemporal dementia.
source: rTg4510 mice express a repressible form of human tau containing the P301L mutation that has been linked with familial frontotemporal dementia.
evidence: This is a description of the mouse model used in the study.

claim: The rTg4510 mouse model represents one of the most well characterised models of tauopathy.
source: They represent one of the most well characterised models of tauopathy (Santacruz et al., 2005; de Calignon et al., 2010; Spires-Jones et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Velocity information can be represented in the brain via the dynamic regulation of the power and frequency of neuronal network oscillations in the theta and gamma frequency bands.
source: Velocity information can be represented in the brain via the dynamic regulation of the power and frequency of neuronal network oscillations in the theta and gamma frequency bands (Ahmed and Mehta, 2012; McFarland et al., 1975; Zheng et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2011; Sławińska and Kasicki, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The profound deficits in spatial memory that occur in response to tau pathologies arise from impaired representation of locomotor speed in the hippocampal formation.
source: We hypothesised that the profound deficits in spatial memory that occur in response to tau pathologies (Booth et al., 2016a; Fu et al., 2017; Ramsden et al., 2005) arise from impaired representation of locomotor speed in the hippocampal formation, ultimately leading to deficits in the encoding of spatial information.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on prior work and their experimental design.

claim: In WT mice, theta oscillation properties followed changes to locomotor activity.
source: As expected, in WT mice, theta oscillation properties followed changes to locomotor activity (Figure 1A/B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A/B.

claim: Similar running speed modulation has been observed in both the fast (60–120 Hz) and slow (30–50 Hz) gamma frequency bands.
source: Similar running speed modulation has been observed in both in the fast (60–120 Hz) and slow (30–50 Hz) gamma frequency bands (Zheng et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The slope of the association between gamma oscillation power and running speed was greater for fast gamma frequencies than slow gamma frequencies in WT mice (slow gamma: 27.1 ± 8.4 mV2/Hz.cm−1, fast gamma: 80.6 ± 19.2 mV2/Hz.cm−1).
source: although the slope of this association was greater for fast gamma frequencies (slow gamma: 27.1 ± 8.4 mV2/Hz.cm−1, fast gamma: 80.6 ± 19.2 mV2/Hz.cm−1; two-way repeated measures ANOVA; Table 1 and Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Table 1 and Figure 1D.

claim: Impairments to the theta oscillatory code for running speed may impair grid cell rhythmicity.
source: Impairments to the theta oscillatory code for running speed may impair grid cell rhythmicity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings.

claim: Extracellularly recorded spike waveforms from interneurons in the mEC have a significantly narrower spike widths when compared to excitatory neurons.
source: Extracellularly recorded spike waveforms from interneurons in the mEC have a significantly narrower spike widths when compared to excitatory neurons (Buetfering et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The probability distributions of single unit spike widths recorded from the dorsal MEC in WT mice had a bimodal distribution.
source: The probability distributions of single unit spike widths recorded from the dorsal MEC in WT mice had a bimodal distribution (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Units with spike widths < 0.35 ms were classed as putative interneurons and those >0.35 ms as putative excitatory cells.
source: Based on this distribution and previously published work (Buetfering et al., 2014), we classed units with spike widths < 0.35 ms as putative interneurons and those >0.35 ms as putative excitatory cells.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on experimental data and prior work.

claim: In the presence of tau pathology, measures of spike width should be met with caution, since the effect of action potential dynamics under these conditions is not necessarily clear.
source: However, it should be noted that in the presence of tau pathology these measures should be met with caution, since the effect of action potential dynamics under these conditions is not necessarily clear.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the interpretation of the data.

claim: Fu et al., 2017 describe no effective impact of tau pathology on HD or border cell firing rates using the rTgTauEC mouse model.
source: Fu et al., 2017 also describe no effective impact of tau pathology on HD or border cell firing rates using the rTgTauEC mouse model.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In the rTgTauEC mouse model, tau pathology was restricted to the MEC, rather than impacting the broader circuits involved in these processes.
source: However, it should be noted that in this case tau pathology was restricted to the MEC, rather than impacting the broader circuits involved in these processes.
evidence: This is a description of a prior study's experimental model.

claim: Some of the pathological and behavioural features observed in the rTg4510 have been associated with the specific transgene insertion sites in this mouse line, rather than tauP301L overexpression per se.
source: In particular, some of the pathological and behavioural features observed in the rTg4510 have been associated with the specific transgene insertion sites in this mouse line, rather than tauP301L overexpression per se (Gamache et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A recently described humanised tau mouse line, generated using gene editing approaches, expresses wild-type tau under endogenous promoters.
source: For example, a recently described humanised tau mouse line, generated using gene editing approaches, expresses wild-type tau under endogenous promoters (Saito et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The humanised tau mouse line does not naturally develop any neuropathological features, but is capable of supporting an accelerated tau pathology when challenged by intracortical injections of human AD brain extract.
source: Whilst this mouse line does not naturally develop any neuropathological features, it is capable of supporting an accelerated tau pathology when challenged by intracortical injections of human AD brain extract (Saito et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Hippocampal place cells could be thought of as conjunctive integrators of multiple spatial (and non-spatial) input streams.
source: Since hippocampal place cells could be thought of as conjunctive integrators of multiple spatial (and non-spatial) input streams, surviving inputs may facilitate encoding of an impoverished spatial representation in these mice (Booth et al., 2016a; Cheng and Ji, 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings based on prior work.

claim: The loss of grid/speed input prevents place cell representation from being anchored to an egocentric spatial reference frame, resulting in decreased spatial stability.
source: However, the loss of grid/speed input prevents this from being anchored to an egocentric spatial reference frame, resulting in decreased spatial stability.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The lateral entorhinal cortex predominately codes for egocentric over allocentric information.
source: It is also possible to consider the role of the lateral entorhinal cortex here, which recent studies have shown to predominately code for egocentric over allocentric information (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Place cells appear before grid cells but mature fully only after grid cell development in neuronal development.
source: Reductions in grid and place field activity may therefore mirror their appearance in neuronal development, where place cells appear before grid cells but mature fully only after grid cell development (Wills et al., 2012; Muessig et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Hippocampal neurons can form place fields in the absence of effective grid cell firing.
source: However, taken together, these data further suggest that hippocampal neurons can form place fields in the absence of effective grid cell firing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Grid cells are proposed to play a key role in path integration.
source: Grid cells are proposed to play a key role in path integration (McNaughton et al., 2006; Burak and Fiete, 2009; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Etienne and Jeffery, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The pronounced cortical shrinkage produced by the rTg4510 model makes the precise positioning of electrode arrays difficult to achieve using standard stereotaxic coordinates.
source: The pronounced cortical shrinkage produced by this model makes the precise positioning of electrode arrays difficult to achieve using standard stereotaxic coordinates.
evidence: This is a methodological observation about the experimental challenges.

claim: Decreased firing alone is not sufficient to account for changes in spatial metrics seen in rTg4510 mice.
source: By down sampling the spike trains of MEC neurons we show that decreased firing alone is not sufficient to account for changes in spatial metrics seen here.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changes to theta rhythmicity are more likely responsible for changes in grid cell periodicity in rTg4510 mice than decreased firing rate.
source: It is more likely, for example, that changes to theta rhythmicity, which often accompany the breakdown of grid cell periodicity, are responsible for changes in these mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The small but significant population increase in HD tuning in rTg4510 mice may reflect unmasking of HD inputs from cells that would have previously displayed grid patterns.
source: It is possible that the small but significant population increase in HD tuning in rTg4510 mice may reflect this unmasking of HD inputs from cells that would have previously displayed grid patterns.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: In rTg4510 mice, HD sensitivity takes a period of time to become fully evident, consistent with disorientation upon entering what should be a familiar environment.
source: This may be such that, in rTg4510 mice, HD sensitivity takes a period of time to become fully evident, consistent with disorientation upon entering what should be a familiar environment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: At fast running speeds, the time window for integration of multimodal sensory information is smaller and it may be necessary to increase the sensitivity of spatially modulated MEC neurons during locomotion.
source: At fast running speeds, the time window for this integration is smaller and it may therefore be necessary to increase the sensitivity of such neurons during locomotion to accurately retrieve spatial associations from memory.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: In rTg4510 mice, theta oscillation power is independent of running speed, meaning that these animals are unable to integrate speed information effectively.
source: In rTg4510 mice, theta oscillation power appears to be independent of running speed meaning that these animals are unable to integrate this information effectively.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings shown in Figure 1.

claim: The hyperactive phenotype in rTg4510 mice may reflect dysregulation of the septohippocampal pathway or dysfunction in motor-related brain regions.
source: This may reflect dysregulation of the septohippocampal pathway, activation of which has been shown to stimulate movement or alternatively may reflect dysfunction in motor-related brain regions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the hyperactive phenotype.

claim: The key finding of this study is that locomotor activity is improperly represented in the hippocampal formation of rTg4510 mice.
source: Nevertheless, whilst it should be noted that rTg4510 mice are experiencing their environment at a generally higher state of arousal, at least in terms of locomotor activity, the key finding of this study is that this locomotor activity is improperly represented in the hippocampal formation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding of the study.

claim: The changes to MEC single unit firing are likely to have profound implications for the impairments in spatial memory observed in rTg4510 mice.
source: The changes to MEC single unit firing are likely to have profound implications for the impairments in spatial memory observed in these mice and suggest observable parameters to assess in dementia patient populations, for example through speed-modulated fMRI signals in virtual environments.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the implications of the findings.
